Is It Time to Get Rid of Gen-Eds?

I'm of a mixed mind on this. There's a difference between education and job training, and the distinction is muddled in college where you can't get one without the other.

If job training is the priority, then I agree. But I'd point out that the skyrocketing price of higher education has more to do with government loans than with useless electives that don't contribute to your targeted expertise.

But then, why stop at college? Why not cut that stuff out of high school as well? Think how much time and money could be saved. Middle school and elementary as well. We could graduate kids at the age of 14! My point is that education has human value even if it doesn't contribute to your expected lifetime earnings. I shudder to think of a country full of worker drones who have been quickly and efficiently trained to skillfully do their jobs but aren't educated enough to cast an intelligent vote. I don't know where the line should be drawn, but throwing out gen ed classes altogether sounds to me like throwing the baby out with the bath water.

I agree with you about the reason why costs are going up, but I would like to see most of the gen ed stuff gone. I took a cultural anthropology class in a auditorium that held 200 people. During lecture I did my math homework, then I had to go to recitation with a smaller group headed by a grad student. They got my money and my time, and I got an 'A' and a 'c' and 'g' on my transcript (Cultural diversity and Global diversity). I don't remember shit from that class. The same goes for Hans Christian Andersen: Literature in Translation course I took.

College composition, computer literacy and critical thinking courses have universal value. The internet makes the cultural stuff obsolete. I've learned more about other cultures by interacting with people on voat / reddit etc. than I did in those classes.

It sounds to me like they did indeed get your money in time in exchange for nothing. Not because anthropology isn't valuable to know a little about, but because you weren't really challenged to learn very much. This is a universal problem in (primarily) public education that I see as a separate issue. I was kind of the same way with my French courses. 12 college hours of French, all that time, money, and 3 months after my last class all I could remember was how to say thank you (merci). Yet, I wonder - if I'd been challenged, if I'd been required to really really put something into it, and prove basic conversational proficiency at the end, it could have broadened my mind today in ways difficult to quantify. For example, I'd give anything to have been able to read about the Charlie Hebdo massacre in actual French, from their perspective.

On the other hand, I did have classes that were an utter waste of time and money regardless of how much I put into them. Political science comes to mind, one of those rare instances where a science major comes face to face with the liberal zealotry that we hear a lot about but don't encounter in our own departments. I remember having to take a course in basic computer literacy which was an utter waste of my time. And music appreciation /eyeroll. But at the same time there were other classes that weren't a waste from a personal point of view. History, in particular. I had a good prof and it woke me up to a lifelong love of history, and my familiarity with it has given me a perspective on world events that I'd hate to have to do without. Same with a couple of others.

So from the point of view of somebody who wants to get trained to do a job and wants to purchase that only, you're right. They should offer you that alternative without all the baggage that comes with it. And those who want to purchase a broader education should be able to, knowing that it is a purchase that won't pay for itself. As I said, I'm not sure you should be forced to take these classes, I'm only saying that I believe they're valuable. And I'd encourage you to look at them that way, even as tedious and useless they may seem at the time.
